events.title: Battle of the Margus
events.summary: Diocletian met Carinus, the legitimate western emperor, on the Margus (Morava) near its confluence with the Danube; Carinus' army was winning when he was murdered by one of his own officers, allegedly a tribune whose wife he had seduced, leaving Diocletian sole emperor.
events.detail: Diocletian retained Carinus' praetorian prefect Aristobulus and most officials, a conciliatory move that contrasted with earlier purges and helped consolidate the regime.
events.locName: River Margus near Margum, Moesia Superior

battle.significance: Last battle of the 'military anarchy'; Diocletian became sole ruler.

events.debate: Date spring or summer 285.

events.title: Maximian raised to Caesar and Augustus
events.summary: Diocletian appointed his fellow Pannonian officer Maximian as Caesar in 285 and as Augustus in 286, creating a dyarchy in which Diocletian took the name Jovius and Maximian Herculius, divine patronage expressing seniority.
events.detail: Maximian was sent to Gaul to suppress the Bagaudae and protect the Rhine, while Diocletian took the Danube and East. The Jovian/Herculian theology, celebrated in the panegyrics of 289 and 291, gave the new collegiate monarchy a sacral foundation independent of dynastic descent.
events.debate: Date of Maximian's elevation to Augustus (1 April 286 or later in 286) and whether he was ever Caesar debated.

events.title: Maximian suppresses the Bagaudae
events.summary: Maximian crushed the Bagaudae, bands of rural rebels in Gaul led by Aelianus and Amandus, who had taken advantage of the collapse of order.
events.detail: The Bagaudae reappear in Gaul and Spain in the fifth century. Older Marxist scholarship saw a peasant revolution; more recent work (Drinkwater) stresses local self-help, banditry and aristocratic leadership. Later tradition placed their stronghold at Saint-Maur-des-Fossés near Paris.
scholarship: Drinkwater, 'Patronage in Roman Gaul and the problem of the Bagaudae', in Wallace-Hadrill (ed.), Patronage in Ancient Society (1989)

events.title: Carausius seizes Britain
events.summary: Mausaeus Carausius, a Menapian commander of the Channel fleet based at Gesoriacum, accused of letting Frankish and Saxon pirates raid in order to seize their loot, was condemned by Maximian and proclaimed himself emperor in Britain and northern Gaul.
events.detail: Carausius' coinage was of unusually good silver and full of Virgilian allusions: RSR (Redeunt Saturnia Regna) and INPCDA (Iam nova progenies caelo demittitur alto), the most literary legends in Roman coinage. He also struck coins of 'Carausius et fratres sui', claiming collegiality with Diocletian and Maximian.
scholarship: Casey, Carausius and Allectus: The British Usurpers (1994)
de la Bédoyère, 'Carausius and the marks RSR and I.N.P.C.D.A.', NC 158 (1998)
events.debate: Date 286 or 287.

events.title: Maximian's failed naval expedition against Carausius
events.summary: A fleet built by Maximian to invade Britain in 289 failed, the panegyrist of 291 hinting at bad weather; for a few years Carausius was tolerated de facto.

events.title: Codex Gregorianus and Codex Hermogenianus
events.summary: The jurists Gregorius and Hermogenianus, working in Diocletian's chancery, compiled the first collections of imperial constitutions (mostly rescripts), the Gregorianus (c. 291-292, from Hadrian onward) and the Hermogenianus (c. 295, Diocletian's own rescripts of 293-294).
events.detail: These private but semi-official codes were the models for the Theodosian Code (438) and Justinian's Codex (529/534), into which much of their content passed. Diocletian's reign is the best-documented in rescripts of any emperor, over 1,200 surviving, reflecting the emperor's role as dispenser of law to ordinary petitioners, including women and slaves.
scholarship: Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (1996, rev. 2000)
Connolly, Lives Behind the Laws (2010)

events.title: Creation of the Tetrarchy
events.summary: On 1 March 293 Maximian appointed Constantius (Chlorus) as his Caesar at Milan and Diocletian appointed Galerius at Sirmium (or Nicomedia), creating a college of two Augusti and two Caesars bound by adoption and marriage.
events.detail: Constantius married Maximian's (step)daughter Theodora, setting aside Helena, mother of Constantine; Galerius married Diocletian's daughter Valeria. Each ruler had his own court, army and prefect, but laws were issued in all four names and the empire remained one. Capitals at Trier, Milan, Sirmium, Thessalonica, Antioch and Nicomedia replaced Rome as centres of government. The word 'Tetrarchy' is modern. Whether Diocletian planned it as a system (with automatic succession and retirement) from the start or improvised it is a central debate; Kolb sees a planned system, while Barnes, Rees and others see more ad hoc arrangements later systematised in Lactantius' narrative.
scholarship: Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Rees, Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (2004)
Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)
events.debate: Planned system or improvisation; place of Galerius' proclamation; whether the Caesars were appointed in 293 or earlier (Galerius possibly in 287 per some).

events.title: Siege of Gesoriacum
events.summary: Constantius, newly made Caesar, blockaded Carausius' continental base at Boulogne with a mole across the harbour mouth and forced its surrender, cutting the usurper off from Gaul.

battle.significance: Isolated Britain and precipitated Carausius' murder.

events.title: Carausius murdered by Allectus
events.summary: After the loss of Boulogne, Carausius was killed by his finance minister (rationalis) Allectus, who ruled Britain for three more years and built a large palace in London, perhaps the structure found under Cannon Street.

events.title: Diocletian's currency reform
events.summary: Around 294 Diocletian created a unified empire-wide coinage: a gold aureus at 60 to the pound, a near-pure silver argenteus at 96 to the pound (reviving Neronian standards), and a large silver-washed bronze 'nummus' (modern 'follis') with the GENIO POPVLI ROMANI reverse, struck at mints marked in a uniform system.
events.detail: Local civic coinages in the East, including Alexandria's tetradrachms, ended (Alexandria by 296-297). The reform did not stop inflation, partly because the state paid and taxed in its own fiduciary coins while gold and silver were hoarded; the doubling of the face value of the nummus in September 301 (Aphrodisias currency edict) and the Price Edict of late 301 were responses.
events.locName: Imperial mints (about 15, from London to Alexandria)
scholarship: Sutherland, RIC VI (1967)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)
events.debate: Exact date (293-296) and denominational values debated.

events.title: Galerius defeats the Carpi; mass resettlement
events.summary: After victories by Galerius, the Carpi of the eastern Carpathians were transplanted wholesale into the empire and settled in Pannonia, a large-scale deportation of the type the Tetrarchs used to repopulate land and supply recruits.
events.debate: Dates of the Carpic victories range 295-297 (Diocletian took Carpicus Maximus several times).

events.title: Constantius recovers Britain
events.summary: Constantius' praetorian prefect Asclepiodotus landed in fog, slipping past Allectus' fleet off the Isle of Wight, burned his boats and defeated and killed Allectus somewhere in southern Britain; Constantius' squadron reached London and saved it from Frankish mercenaries.
events.detail: The famous gold medallion from the Arras (Beaurains) hoard shows Constantius on horseback before a kneeling Londinium with the legend REDDITOR LVCIS AETERNAE ('restorer of the eternal light').

events.title: Diocletian's new tax system (capitatio-iugatio and the indiction)
events.summary: An edict of the prefect of Egypt Aristius Optatus dated 16 March 297 announces a new empire-wide assessment of land (iuga) and people (capita) to calculate annual requisitions in kind, set in a regular budget, the indiction.
events.detail: The system rationalised the improvised levies (annona) of the third century into a predictable annual tax, eventually reassessed on a fifteen-year indiction cycle that became a standard dating system into the Middle Ages (first cycle counted from 312). Assessment units varied regionally (iugum in Syria, millena in Italy, centuria in Africa). Lactantius' complaint that there were more tax collectors than taxpayers reflects the expanded bureaucracy, perhaps 30,000 officials in the fourth century.
scholarship: Carrié, 'Dioclétien et la fiscalité', AnTard 2 (1994)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)
events.debate: Whether capitatio and iugatio were separate or merged taxes, and how uniform the system was, remain debated.

events.title: Diocletian's provincial reorganisation and the dioceses
events.summary: Diocletian roughly doubled the number of provinces from about 50 to about 100, separated civil governors from military commanders (duces), included Italy in the provincial system, and grouped provinces into twelve dioceses under vicarii responsible to the praetorian prefects.
events.detail: The Laterculus Veronensis (Verona List), a seventh-century copy of a list dated c. 303-314, gives the twelve dioceses: Oriens, Pontica, Asiana, Thraciae, Moesiae, Pannoniae, Britanniae, Galliae, Viennensis, Italia, Hispaniae and Africa. Smaller provinces made revolts harder and taxation more intrusive. Italy lost its fiscal privileges (except the suburbicarian region around Rome, whose status is debated), being divided into provinces under correctores. Recent work (Zuckerman) dates the dioceses to c. 313-314 under Constantine and Licinius rather than to Diocletian.
scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982), ch. 12-13
Zuckerman, 'Sur la liste de Vérone et la province de Grande Arménie', TravMém 14 (2002)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964)
events.debate: The date of the dioceses (c. 297 vs c. 313-314) and the exact list of provinces are disputed.

events.title: Revolt of Domitius Domitianus and siege of Alexandria
events.summary: Lucius Domitius Domitianus, with his corrector Aurelius Achilleus, revolted in Egypt in 297, perhaps provoked by the new tax census; Diocletian came in person, besieged Alexandria for eight months, cut the aqueducts, and after its fall vowed to kill until the blood reached his horse's knees.
events.detail: According to the legend, his horse stumbled at the city gate, staining its knees, and the grateful Alexandrians set up a statue of the horse. The tall column known as 'Pompey's Pillar' was erected in honour of Diocletian around 298, probably for his provision of grain to the city. Busiris and Coptos, which had joined the revolt, were razed.

battle.significance: Ended the last major revolt of Roman Egypt; followed by Diocletian's reorganisation of Egypt into separate provinces.

events.debate: Relationship of Domitianus and Achilleus (same revolt, successive leaders) and chronology (297-298) disputed.

events.title: Diocletian withdraws from the Dodecaschoenus
events.summary: Visiting Upper Egypt, Diocletian withdrew the frontier from the Dodecaschoenus to Philae and the First Cataract, settling Nobatae in the evacuated zone as a buffer against the Blemmyes and paying both peoples annual subsidies.
events.detail: Procopius records the arrangement, including shared temples at Philae for the Isis cult, which continued until Justinian closed them c. 537.

events.title: Battle of Callinicum (Galerius' defeat)
events.summary: Narseh, who had seized the Persian throne in 293, invaded Roman Armenia and Mesopotamia; Galerius, attacking with too small a force, was defeated between Callinicum and Carrhae.
events.detail: Ammianus and others tell that Diocletian, in his carriage at Antioch, made Galerius walk a mile in front of it in his purple, a humiliation that Galerius turned into a determination to win; the story's meaning (punishment or ceremonial) is debated.

battle.significance: Prompted the reinforcement of Galerius with Danubian troops for the decisive campaign of 298.

events.debate: Date 296 or 297.

events.title: Galerius' victory in Armenia
events.summary: With a new army of Danubian veterans, Galerius advanced through Armenia, personally reconnoitred the Persian camp and fell on Narseh by surprise, routing his army and capturing his treasury, harem, wife Arsane and children.
events.detail: Galerius' arch at Thessalonica depicts the battle, including a duel-like encounter between Galerius and Narseh. Galerius then advanced down the Tigris through Media and Adiabene and possibly took Ctesiphon. The captured royal women became the key bargaining chip in the peace of 299.
events.locName: Armenia, probably between Satala and Erzurum

battle.significance: Greatest Roman victory over the Sasanians before Heraclius.

scholarship: Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)
Dodgeon and Lieu (1991)
events.debate: Site unknown; 'Satala' is a convenient modern label. Date 298 (some 297).

events.title: Peace of Nisibis
events.summary: Diocletian's envoy Sicorius Probus imposed terms on Narseh: Persia ceded five regions beyond the Tigris (Arzanene, Moxoene, Zabdicene, Rehimene and Corduene), recognised Roman control of Armenia (border at Zintha) and Iberia, and accepted Nisibis as the sole point of trade exchange.
events.detail: Peter the Patrician, our main source, preserves the negotiations: the Persian envoy Apharban called Rome and Persia the two eyes of the world. The treaty gave Rome its best eastern frontier ever and forty years of peace, until Shapur II reopened war. Jovian's surrender of the Transtigritane regions and Nisibis in 363 reversed it.
scholarship: Blockley, 'The Romano-Persian peace treaties of AD 299 and 363', Florilegium 6 (1984)
Winter, Die sasanidisch-römischen Friedensverträge des 3. Jahrhunderts n. Chr. (1988)
events.debate: The list of five regions differs between Peter and Ammianus; date 298 or 299.

events.title: Battles of Lingones and Vindonissa
events.summary: Constantius, nearly captured and hauled over the walls of Lingones (Langres) by a rope, defeated the Alamanni outside the city the same day, killing 60,000 according to Eutropius, and won a second victory near Vindonissa.

battle.significance: Secured the upper Rhine for a generation.

events.debate: Date 298 or 302.

events.title: Strata Diocletiana and the fortified eastern frontier
events.summary: Diocletian built or rebuilt a chain of forts along a military road from north-east Arabia through Damascus and Palmyra to Sura on the Euphrates, marked by milestones naming the Strata Diocletiana.
events.detail: The programme, along with new legions (by now smaller units of perhaps 1,000-2,000 men) and quadriburgia, reflects the tetrarchic investment in frontier defence that Zosimus contrasts with Constantine's withdrawal of troops into cities.
events.locName: Syrian desert from Bostra to Sura via Palmyra
scholarship: Bowersock, Roman Arabia (1983)
Parker, Romans and Saracens (1986)

events.title: Diocletian's edict against the Manichaeans
events.summary: Diocletian ordered the leaders of the Manichaeans burned with their books and their followers executed or sent to the mines, condemning the sect as a Persian import that corrupted the 'modest and tranquil Roman people'.
events.locName: Rescript to the proconsul of Africa
events.debate: Date 297 or 302 depends on the identification of the proconsul Julianus and Diocletian's itinerary.

events.title: Edict on Maximum Prices
events.summary: Issued between 20 November and 9 December 301 in the names of all four Tetrarchs, the Edictum de pretiis rerum venalium fixed maximum prices and wages for over 1,200 goods and services, from wheat and wine to lion skins, freight charges and a lawyer's fee, on pain of death.
events.detail: Its preamble denounces the 'unbridled greed' of profiteers who follow the armies. Known from over 130 fragments of inscriptions, mostly from the Greek East (Aphrodisias, Stratonicea, Tegea and elsewhere), with prices in 'denarii communes'. Examples: a modius castrensis of wheat 100 denarii; farm labourer 25 denarii a day with keep; a pound of purple silk 150,000. Lactantius says it caused goods to disappear from markets and much bloodshed, and was soon abandoned. Modern historians value it as the single richest economic document from antiquity, while debating whether its figures reflect real prices.
events.locName: Issued probably from Nicomedia; copies across the eastern provinces

sources.w: Edictum Diocletiani de pretiis rerum venalium

scholarship: Lauffer, Diokletians Preisedikt (1971)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)
Crawford and Reynolds, 'The Aphrodisias copy of Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices', ZPE 26 (1977)
events.debate: Whether the edict was ever seriously enforced, and whether it was applied in the West, are disputed; Lactantius is hostile.

events.title: Currency edict of 301 (Aphrodisias)
events.summary: An edict, known from an inscription at Aphrodisias and effective 1 September 301, retariffed the coinage, apparently doubling the face value of the nummus and the argenteus, a revaluation that preceded the Price Edict by three months.
events.debate: Exact values in the damaged text are disputed.

events.title: Conversion of Armenia under Tiridates III
events.summary: King Tiridates III of Armenia, restored by Rome, accepted Christianity through the preaching of Gregory the Illuminator, who was consecrated bishop at Caesarea in Cappadocia; Armenia claims to be the first Christian kingdom.
events.detail: Armenian tradition (Agathangelos) dates the conversion to 301, after Gregory's thirteen years in a pit at Khor Virap and the king's transformation into a boar. Most modern scholars prefer c. 314, after the Edict of Milan and Galerius' and Maximinus' persecutions, which Eusebius says included a war by Maximinus against Christian Armenians.
scholarship: Garsoïan, in Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times I (1997)
events.debate: Date 301 (tradition) vs c. 314 (most scholars).

events.title: The Great Persecution begins
events.summary: On the feast of the Terminalia, 23 February 303, soldiers demolished the church of Nicomedia, visible from the palace; the next day an edict ordered churches destroyed, scriptures surrendered and burned, Christian meetings banned and Christians of rank stripped of privileges.
events.detail: Three further edicts followed: arrest of clergy, release of clergy who sacrificed, and (spring 304) a general order for all to sacrifice. Lactantius blames Galerius and an oracle of Apollo at Didyma for the decision. Enforcement varied enormously: Constantius in Gaul and Britain went no further than pulling down some churches, while the East under Galerius and Maximinus Daia suffered persecution until 311 and, intermittently, 313. Eusebius' Martyrs of Palestine counts some 90 executions there. The surrender of scriptures created the 'traditores' problem that split the African church into Donatists and Catholics.
scholarship: de Ste. Croix, 'Aspects of the Great Persecution', HTR 47 (1954)
Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Corcoran, 'Before Constantine', in Lenski (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006/2012)
events.debate: Lactantius and Eusebius are partisan Christian sources writing after the persecutors' defeat; Galerius' role may be exaggerated to exculpate Diocletian or vice versa. Numbers of martyrs are uncertain.

events.title: Diocletian's vicennalia in Rome
events.summary: Diocletian visited Rome, probably for the only time, to celebrate his twentieth anniversary and a joint triumph with Maximian; the Decennalia base of the Tetrarchs in the Forum survives. Irritated by Roman freedom of speech, he left in December before taking up his consulship.

events.title: Baths of Diocletian in Rome
events.summary: Maximian began, in Diocletian's name, the largest baths ever built in Rome, covering 13 hectares on the Viminal, dedicated 305-306; Michelangelo converted the frigidarium into the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli.

events.title: Diocletian's palace at Spalatum
events.summary: Diocletian built a fortified retirement palace near Salona on the Dalmatian coast, a 215 x 180 m enclosure combining fortress plan, residence, mausoleum (now Split cathedral) and temple (now baptistery), which became the nucleus of the city of Split.
events.detail: The peristyle with its arcuated colonnades and the palace's courtly architecture influenced late antique and Renaissance taste (Robert Adam's 1764 publication). Comparable tetrarchic palace-mausolea are Galerius' Felix Romuliana (Gamzigrad) and the Thessalonica complex.
scholarship: Wilkes, Diocletian's Palace, Split (1986)

events.title: Synod of Elvira
events.summary: Nineteen Spanish bishops, including Ossius of Corduba, met at Iliberris (Granada) and issued 81 canons, the earliest surviving disciplinary code of a church council, including clerical celibacy, bans on images painted on church walls and on marriage of Christian girls to Jews or pagans.

sources.w: Canons of the Council of Elvira

events.debate: Date anywhere from c. 295 to 314; the canon collection may be a later compilation (Meigne, Vilella).

events.title: Abdication of Diocletian and Maximian
events.summary: On 1 May 305 Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan simultaneously abdicated; Constantius and Galerius became Augusti, and the new Caesars were Galerius' protégés Severus and Maximinus Daia, passing over Constantine and Maxentius, the sons of emperors.
events.detail: Lactantius describes the assembled army at Nicomedia expecting Constantine to be named and being astonished when Galerius pushed forward Maximinus. Diocletian retired to Spalatum to grow cabbages (as he later told Maximian, who urged him to resume power in 308). The voluntary abdication of a Roman emperor was unprecedented; the exclusion of dynastic heirs proved fatal to the system within eighteen months.
events.locName: Hill three miles from Nicomedia; Mediolanum

events.title: Constantine proclaimed at Eboracum
events.summary: Constantius I died at York after a campaign against the Picts, and his army, prompted by the Alamannic king Crocus, proclaimed his son Constantine Augustus; Galerius grudgingly recognised him as Caesar.
events.detail: Constantine had escaped Galerius' court in 305, reportedly hamstringing the post-horses behind him. His accession broke the tetrarchic principle of merit-appointment in favour of heredity and began the dynasty that ruled until 363.

events.title: Maxentius seizes Rome
events.summary: Angered by Galerius' plan to extend the census and taxation to the city of Rome and to abolish the Praetorian Guard, the Praetorians and people proclaimed Maximian's son Maxentius princeps, and Maximian came out of retirement to support him.
events.detail: Maxentius styled himself 'conservator urbis suae' and lavished building on Rome: the Basilica Nova, the rebuilt Temple of Venus and Roma, and the villa, circus and mausoleum on the Via Appia.

events.title: Severus' invasion of Italy and death
events.summary: Severus, sent by Galerius against Maxentius, advanced on Rome but his troops, many of them former soldiers of Maximian, deserted; he fled to Ravenna, surrendered on promise of his life, and was later killed or forced to suicide at Tres Tabernae.

events.title: Galerius' failed invasion of Italy
events.summary: Galerius marched on Rome in summer 307 but, finding the city too large and well defended to besiege and his troops wavering, retreated, allowing his army to plunder Italy on the way.

events.title: Constantine marries Fausta and is made Augustus by Maximian
events.summary: At Trier, Maximian gave his daughter Fausta to Constantine in marriage and named him Augustus, an alliance celebrated in a panegyric (Pan. Lat. 7(6)) that describes a painting of the betrothal at Aquileia.

events.title: Conference of Carnuntum
events.summary: Galerius summoned Diocletian from retirement to Carnuntum; Maximian was forced to abdicate again, Licinius was made Augustus of the West directly, Constantine was demoted to Caesar, and Maxentius was declared a public enemy.
events.detail: Diocletian refused to resume power, replying that if Maximian could see the cabbages he grew at Salona he would never urge it. An altar to Mithras 'fautor imperii sui' dedicated by the emperors at Carnuntum survives. The settlement failed at once: Maximinus Daia and Constantine both claimed the Augustan title in 309-310.

events.title: Revolt of Domitius Alexander in Africa
events.summary: Lucius Domitius Alexander, vicarius of Africa, rebelled against Maxentius, cutting Rome's grain supply; Maxentius' praetorian prefect Rufius Volusianus crushed him around 310 and sacked Carthage and Cirta.
events.detail: Cirta was rebuilt by Constantine and renamed Constantina (Constantine, Algeria). The famine in Rome during the revolt weakened Maxentius' popularity.

events.title: Revolt and death of Maximian at Massilia
events.summary: Living at Constantine's court, Maximian proclaimed himself emperor again at Arles while Constantine was on the Rhine; Constantine marched south, besieged him in Massilia and Maximian was forced to hang himself.
events.detail: Lactantius adds a second plot in which Maximian tried to murder Constantine in bed and killed a eunuch substitute. Constantine then abandoned his Herculian descent and claimed descent from Claudius II, announced in the panegyric of 310.

events.title: Constantine's 'pagan vision' at Grand
events.summary: The panegyrist of 310 describes Constantine visiting a temple of Apollo (probably at Grand in the Vosges), where he saw Apollo with Victory offering him laurel wreaths each bearing the sign XXX, foretelling a thirty-year reign.
events.detail: Peter Weiss argued that what Constantine actually saw was a solar halo phenomenon, later reinterpreted as the Christian vision reported by Eusebius; others keep the 310 and 312 visions distinct. Constantine's coinage honoured Sol Invictus as 'comes' until the early 320s.
scholarship: Weiss, 'The vision of Constantine', JRA 16 (2003)
Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power (2011)
events.debate: Identification of the temple; relation to the later Christian vision.

events.title: Constantine introduces the solidus
events.summary: Around 309-310, at the Trier mint, Constantine began striking a lighter gold coin at 72 to the Roman pound (c. 4.5 g), the solidus, which became the stable standard of the late Roman and Byzantine world for some 700 years.
events.detail: Funded partly by confiscated temple treasures after 324, the solidus circulated in large volumes and taxes were increasingly commuted into gold (adaeratio), creating, in Jairus Banaji's analysis, a gold-based aristocracy and a deep divide between gold-holders and those paid in debased bronze. Its fineness was maintained until the eleventh century, earning it the nickname 'dollar of the Middle Ages'.
scholarship: Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity (2001)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)
Bruun, RIC VII (1966)
events.debate: Date (309 or 310) and whether introduced initially only in Constantine's territories (extended east after 324).

events.title: Galerius' edict of toleration and death
events.summary: Dying of a horrible disease (Lactantius describes his body consumed by worms), Galerius issued an edict, posted at Nicomedia on 30 April 311, ending the persecution and permitting Christians to 'exist again and hold their meetings' on condition they pray to their god for the emperors' safety; he died days later.
events.detail: The edict acknowledges failure: many Christians had neither returned to the gods nor worshipped their own god. Maximinus Daia complied only briefly and resumed persecution in late 311 with petitions from cities requesting the expulsion of Christians (an inscription from Arycanda survives).
events.debate: Lactantius' gloating account of Galerius' illness is a stock 'death of the persecutor' motif.

events.title: Outbreak of the Donatist schism
events.summary: The consecration of Caecilian as bishop of Carthage by Felix of Abthugni, accused of being a traditor in the persecution, was rejected by Numidian bishops, who elected Majorinus and then Donatus; the African church split into two hierarchies for over a century.
events.detail: The dissidents appealed to Constantine in 313, prompting the Council of Rome (313) and Council of Arles (314), both of which upheld Caecilian. Constantine's attempt at coercion (317-321) failed and he conceded toleration. The Donatists, rigorist and rooted in Numidia, saw themselves as the church of martyrs; violent rural partisans, the Circumcellions, later attached themselves to the movement. The schism lasted until the conference of Carthage in 411 and beyond.
scholarship: Frend, The Donatist Church (1952)
Shaw, Sacred Violence (2011)
events.debate: Date of Caecilian's election (307/8 or 311/312) disputed.

events.title: Basilica Nova of Maxentius
events.summary: Maxentius built the vast Basilica Nova on the Velia with three cross-vaulted bays over a 25 m-wide nave, the last great vaulted civic building of pagan Rome, completed by Constantine, who placed his colossal seated statue (whose head and hand survive in the Capitoline Museums) in a new apse.
